sections.overview: This small swallow breeds across Europe, North Africa and temperate Asia, then migrates to sub-Saharan Africa following seasonal supplies of flying insects.
sections.identification: Adults average about 13 cm long, with a 26–29 cm wingspan; the sexes look alike. Blue-black upperparts, white rump and belly, and a shallowly forked tail mark the species. Unlike the barn swallow, it has no red throat or long tail streamers; juveniles are duller. British adults average about 17.8 g; the species is about 13 cm long with a 26–29 cm wingspan.
sections.habitat: It hunts over open country, meadows, farmland and water, where flying insects are accessible. It nests on cliffs or, commonly, outside buildings and bridges beneath sheltered overhangs. British surveys in 2016–17 found lower breeding success on PVC than on brick, concrete or wood, with more nest collapses: the supporting surface matters as well as available mud.
sections.diet: It captures small insects and spiders in flight. Flies and aphids are common breeding-season prey; flying ants also contribute on African wintering grounds.
sections.behavior: They often forage in loose groups above water and nest socially in colonies. Soft twittering maintains contact, while sharper alarm calls alert nearby birds to danger.
sections.reproduction: After courtship, both partners build or repair a closed mud nest under an eave, leaving a small entrance; grasses and hair soften its lining. The female lays usually four or five eggs, incubated by the pair for about two weeks. Helpless hatchlings stay in the nest for roughly three to four weeks, then parents feed them for about another week. Mud mixed with saliva dries into a durable cement, allowing nests to be reused in successive years. Two broods in a season are usual in Britain.
sections.ecology: It eats flying insects, is prey for the Eurasian hobby, and its reused mud nests can harbour fleas and mites.
sections.conservation: The LPO reports a 26% decline in European breeding numbers from 1980 to 2019; pesticides, poor weather, scarce mud and nest destruction are local pressures. This regional trend differs from the global IUCN assessment: dated 1 October 2016 and amended in 2017, it classed the species as Least Concern.
